why: He was not selling coffee, he was renting real estate by the hour. why: Analog and RF semiconductors are a business of accumulated process recipes, not transistor counts, so they do not commoditise the way digital logic does. Buying a neglected defence-and-telecom chip house cheaply in 2008 and refitting it for optical and 5G front ends captured a supply niche that the large fabs had abandoned.
obst: MACOM was a loss-making orphan inside Cobham when GaAs Labs bought control in 2008; the company later mis-timed a bet on datacenter optics and its shares fell by more than two thirds in 2018 and 2019, and John Ocampo died in 2023 leaving her the controlling holder.
turn: The 2008 acquisition of MACOM out of Cobham, which turned a one-time chip exit into a permanent controlling stake in a listed semiconductor company.

obst: He carried more than 5 billion dollars of high-yield debt against businesses with no earnings, was repeatedly told cellular would stay a car-phone niche, and his brother Keith died in 1989; Nextel was near bankruptcy when he recapitalised it in 1995 and Clearwire ultimately sold to Sprint at a fraction of its peak.

s: Impinj DEF 14A of 16 Apr 2026: 752,164 shares, 2.5 percent; PI closed 165.54 dollars on 21 August 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial share count times market price
did: A Caltech-trained researcher and University of Washington professor, he co-founded Impinj in 2000 to commercialise low-power silicon for passive RFID tags, wrote much of the UHF Gen2 standard the industry adopted, took the company public in 2016 and has run it since as chief executive.
why: Impinj sells both the tag chip and the reader chip, so it earns on every item tagged and every gate that reads it. Writing the Gen2 standard meant the interoperability rules were built around its silicon, and once Walmart, Zara and Delta mandated item-level tagging the volume ramp was regulatory rather than competitive.
obst: Impinj spent sixteen years and several near-death funding rounds waiting for RFID adoption after the 2003 Walmart mandate failed to materialise; a long patent war with NXP ran from 2019 to 2024, and the shares halved in 2022 on an inventory correction at its largest customers.
turn: The 2020s apparel and logistics mandates from Walmart, Zara owner Inditex and the airlines, which finally moved tag volumes from hundreds of millions to tens of billions a year.

s: Remitly DEF 14A of 24 Apr 2026: 4,386,668 shares, 2.1 percent; RELY closed 26.67 dollars on 21 August 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial share count times market price
did: Co-founded the social book-cataloguing site Shelfari, sold it to Amazon in 2008 and ran it there, then co-founded Remitly in Seattle in 2011 as chief product officer, later chief operating officer and vice chair, building the customer-facing side of a remittance app now handling more than 10 million active users.
why: Remittance customers are choosing under fear, not price alone: a failed transfer means a family does not eat. Hug built the product around delivery certainty and status transparency rather than the lowest headline rate, which produced retention that let the company spend more to acquire each sender than rivals could.
obst: Shelfari was bought by Amazon and eventually shut down in 2016, an exit that produced no fortune; at Remitly the early product lost money on fraud in the Philippine corridor and had to be rebuilt corridor by corridor under state money-transmitter licensing.
turn: The 2016 shift from a single corridor to a licensed multi-corridor platform, which made every new country an incremental build rather than a new company.

s: Absci DEF 14A of 22 Apr 2026: 11,371,214 shares, 7.20 percent; ABSI closed 9.55 dollars on 21 August 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial share count times market price
did: Founded Absci in 2011 at 21 with a biology degree and no company experience, built a system that screens billions of protein variants in E. coli and later paired it with generative AI to design antibodies de novo; took it public in 2021 and signed development deals with AstraZeneca, Merck and Eli Lilly.
why: Antibody discovery normally means immunising animals and screening whatever the immune system happens to produce. Absci generates and tests candidates in bacteria, so the search space is set by computation rather than biology, and the wet-lab data it produces retrains the model, which is a data advantage a pure software firm cannot buy.
obst: He spent the first years running the company out of Vancouver, Washington on grants and small rounds, pivoted from a protein-production tools business to drug creation, and watched the shares fall from a 16 dollar IPO price to about 2 dollars before clinical data on ABS-201 and an Eli Lilly investment revived them.
turn: The 2023 pivot to generative AI antibody design, which converted a screening-services business into a partner biotech pharmaceutical companies pay milestones to.
